item.title: Architecture
item.description:
Coding agents need to push code and open pull requests. Giving them a developer’s credentials makes every agent action look like the developer’s, and a prompt injection then holds everything the developer can do. Token Broker gives the agent its own GitHub identity instead: a GitHub App. Its commits and pull requests show up as <app>[bot] and need a human review.

One key, one place

An app can mint installation tokens only with its private key. The key lives in the broker alone. Agents, containers and workstations ask the broker for a token and never see the key.

Two auth paths

Caller Proves identity with Endpoint
Developer (local agent) user token of a permission-less login app, via device flow POST /token
GitHub Actions workflow the workflow’s OIDC token POST /token/actions (or /token)
  • Developer. agent-token --login runs GitHub’s device flow with the login app, an app with no permissions at all. It only proves who the developer is. The login token lives 8 hours in the developer’s cache. The broker asks GitHub whether that user has write access to the requested repository and refuses otherwise: a developer can hand the agent only repositories they could push to themselves.
  • Workflow. The workflow requests an OIDC token with the audience the broker expects and sends it to the broker. The broker verifies it against GitHub’s issuer. A workflow gets a token only for the repository it runs in, optionally limited to certain refs and workflows. /token/actions accepts nothing but these tokens, so a public route can forward it while everything else stays internal.

What the token is

In both cases the broker then:

  1. checks that the repository belongs to one of the configured organizations;
  2. signs an app JWT with the private key and looks up the app’s installation on the repository, refusing if the app is not installed there;
  3. mints an installation token for that one repository, with the configured permissions (default: contents, pull requests and issues write, metadata read).

The token lives one hour. Clients fetch tokens on demand, per repository, at the moment git, gh or the GitHub MCP server need one, and cache them. Every issued or denied token is logged: who, which repository, why.

Parts

  • Broker: a small stateless Go service, run as a Helm chart with two replicas. It has no database and never calls the Kubernetes API.
  • Client scripts: agent-token and the helpers built on it. See Client commands.
  • Claude Code plugin, Dev Container Feature and agent-run: three ways to put the client into the agent’s environment. See Getting started.

Setup details: Set up the GitHub Apps. Endpoints and errors: Endpoints.

item.title: Security model
item.description:
What the agent never sees

  • The agent app’s private key and the login app’s client secret. They exist only in the broker.
  • The developer’s own credentials. Agent commits and API calls use agent tokens, so they cannot act as the developer.

An agent token is limited to one repository, lives one hour and carries only the configured permissions. Metadata aside, the default is contents, pull requests and issues. It has no workflow, administration, secrets or status permissions, so it cannot edit CI, manage the repository or report a required check as green.

Humans stay in the loop

The agent app can approve pull requests, and with contents write its approvals would count toward required reviews. Every repository it is installed on must therefore require a code owner review and have a CODEOWNERS file that names human teams: bots cannot be code owners. See Set review rules.

The plugin is a guardrail, not a sandbox

The Claude Code plugin tells Claude to use agent tokens and blocks git commit, git push and a bare gh by matching command text. A command like env git push, /usr/bin/git push or a script that pushes gets through and uses the developer’s credentials. The block also follows the session, not the directory: after a cd into another repository it still applies, and a session started outside an agent-token repository stays unguarded.

Repository admins can edit topics by hand. A wrong topic costs a failed call and nothing more, because the broker refuses tokens where the app is not installed.

Host versus container

Host with the plugin Container or Dev Container
Developer credentials (~/.ssh, gh login) reachable by the agent not mounted
Enforcement command-text guard the container’s contents
Network unrestricted Dev Container: egress firewall with an allowlist

On the host, deny the agent read access to ~/.ssh, ~/.config/gh and ~/.cache/agent-token. For isolation run the agent with agent-run or in the Dev Container. The Dev Container’s firewall cannot be lifted by the agent, but your forwarded SSH agent can still sign; use agent-run for full isolation. Skipping Claude’s permission prompts is reasonable only with the firewall active.

Exposure of the broker

The device-flow client ID is public, so a reachable broker invites phishing. Keep /token internal. Only /token/actions is built for public exposure: it accepts Actions OIDC tokens and nothing else. GitHub never calls the broker; it needs outbound access to api.github.com and token.actions.githubusercontent.com only. Run it behind TLS.

Limits: commits made with local git are unsigned, so on branches that require signatures use agent-commit or squash-merge.
